case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal candidates have Article III standing to challenge Illinois’s rule counting certain mail-in ballots received after the federally designated Election Day for federal offices.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Day statutes: 2 U.S.C. § 1 (House elections), 2 U.S.C. § 7 (Senate elections), 3 U.S.C. § 1 and § 21(1) (presidential electors); and Illinois’s ballot-receipt statute, 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c) (2025), requiring counting of some vote-by-mail ballots received up to 14 days after Election Day if postmarked or certified as on/before Election Day.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (federal candidates) argue they are among the direct and predictable objects of Illinois’s ballot-counting deadline regime because the rules govern what votes are counted in their elections; counting ballots received after the single federal Election Day unlawfully alters the election rules and creates concrete competitive harms (e.g., dilution/offset of timely votes, increased risk of losing, and campaign/strategy/resource burdens). They contend ordinary standing principles for regulated parties apply: candidates need not prove a razor-thin race or certain loss; a substantial risk of harm suffices, and pre-election clarity is essential to avoid post-election remedial chaos.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the candidates lack Article III standing because any alleged injury is speculative and generalized: counting a subset of late-arriving ballots does not concretely injure a candidate absent plausible allegations that such ballots could change the election outcome (especially where margins are not close), and the alleged harm is better characterized as a voter-focused policy choice rather than a direct regulation of candidates. They also emphasize limits on procedural-injury and risk-of-harm standing (to avoid opening federal courts to broad election-administration challenges by disappointed or ideologically motivated plaintiffs).
key_precedents: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) (standing limits on risk/procedural injury)
Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510 (1925) (standing of regulated/affected parties—referenced by analogy in argument)
CBS, Inc. v. FCC, 453 U.S. 367 (1981) (standing of parties affected by regulatory regimes—referenced by analogy in argument)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that candidates are the direct objects of election rules and need pre-election clarity, and that Article III does not require proof a race will be razor-thin. But his reframing of the injury as “forced participation in an allegedly unlawful counting regime” risks collapsing Clapper and TransUnion’s substantial-risk requirement into a merits claim—if the mere existence of a contested rule in one’s election sufficed, Gill’s particularization limit would do little work. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Illinois does not regulate candidates’ conduct or threaten enforcement; the alleged competitive harm still depends on contingencies (volume, distribution, and margin sensitivity) that are not plausibly alleged as to these petitioners’ districts. Consistent with judicial minimalism and institutional legitimacy, the narrow course is to affirm on standing and leave the Election Day statute merits for a record with concrete, race-specific facts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I understand the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s concern that Clapper/TransUnion require a “substantial risk” supported by district-specific allegations, but that framework cannot be allowed to displace Article III’s original public meaning: the injury here is the compelled participation in an election conducted under an allegedly unlawful counting rule governing petitioners’ own federal contests, not a probabilistic showing about margin sensitivity. Justice Barrett’s “no limiting principle” point fails under an originalist methodology because the limiting principle is particularization—these are candidates in the affected elections—so this is not the undifferentiated statewide grievance Gill v. Whitford addressed. Nor is it dispositive, as Justice Kagan urges, that there is no enforcement threat; historically, standing has never been confined to regulated-party or pre-enforcement paradigms where the government’s binding rules alter the legal conditions of a plaintiff’s own contest. Clapper’s chain-of-contingencies rationale is inapt because the operative change in the rules of what votes will be counted after the federally set Election Day is itself imminent and concrete, even if one cannot yet quantify precisely how many ballots will arrive late or how they will break.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that candidates are the “predictable objects” of election-administration rules in their own races and that Article III does not require certainty or proof of a razor-thin margin. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, this is not a pre-enforcement case: Illinois’s receipt rule does not regulate petitioners’ conduct or threaten enforcement, and the asserted competitive harm depends on contingent third-party behavior (how many late ballots arrive, where they come from, and whether any petitioner’s margin is plausibly affected). Under Clapper and TransUnion, forward-looking relief still requires a substantial, non-speculative risk of concrete harm, and the pleadings here lack the district- or contest-specific facts that Gill v. Whitford demands to move beyond an abstract grievance about election rules. Accepting standing on this record would effectively authorize generalized federal oversight of state ballot-counting practices whenever a candidate alleges illegality, and I do not see a workable limiting principle consistent with Article III.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that candidates are not bringing an undifferentiated statewide grievance like Gill v. Whitford and need not show they will probably lose to have standing, but his reframing of the injury as “forced participation in an allegedly unlawful counting regime” still does not supply the concrete, particularized harm Clapper and TransUnion require for forward-looking relief. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Illinois is not regulating petitioners’ conduct or threatening enforcement; the alleged competitive injury materializes only if late-arriving ballots are numerous, geographically concentrated in these petitioners’ districts, and margin-relevant—facts absent from the pleadings. Without those district-tethered allegations, recognizing standing would collapse Article III’s limiting principle and predictably invite disruptive pre-election federal supervision of routine election administration, with real burdens on voters who depend on mail voting. I would therefore affirm on standing and leave the Election Day statutes for a record showing a substantial, non-speculative risk in a particular contest.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that standing is not limited to enforcement threats and that candidates are the predictable objects of election rules in their own races. But his reframing of the injury as “forced participation in an allegedly unlawful counting regime” is too abstract under Clapper and TransUnion: it collapses the concreteness inquiry into the merits and would confer standing whenever a plaintiff alleges illegality in election administration, the very limiting-principle problem Justice Barrett flags. Because Illinois’s receipt rule affects these petitioners only through contingencies (volume, distribution, and margin sensitivity) and the pleadings supply no race-specific facts to make the risk “substantial,” I agree with the Chief Justice that Gill’s particularization concerns counsel affirming on standing and leaving the statutory merits for a record tethered to identifiable contests. Pragmatically, that narrower disposition preserves Article III limits while still allowing future plaintiffs to proceed when they can plausibly allege a concrete, district-specific exposure to outcome-relevant harm.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not demand proof an election will be razor-thin, and that candidates are the predictable objects of vote-counting rules in their own races. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Clapper and TransUnion still require either a concrete injury or at least a pleaded, non-speculative “substantial risk,” and these petitioners offer no district-specific allegations about late-ballot volumes, likely margins, or distributional facts that would particularize the asserted “competitive injury” under Gill. I also agree with Justice Kagan that the pre-enforcement/regulated-party analogy breaks down because Illinois is not regulating petitioners’ conduct or threatening sanctions; the asserted harm depends on multiple contingencies involving third-party ballots. However important the Election Day statutes’ merits may be, they cannot relax Article III’s limits on this thin record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not require petitioners to show their races will be razor-thin or that the challenged rule will probably change the outcome; I agree standing cannot be limited to outcome-determinative harm. But the Chief Justice’s Clapper/TransUnion framework still requires a plausible, particularized “substantial risk” of concrete competitive injury, and on these pleadings the asserted harm turns on an unalleged chain—how many late ballots arrive, where they are cast, and whether those numbers could matter in any petitioner’s specific contest—making this look like the generalized election-administration grievance Gill cautions against. Justice Barrett’s limiting-principle concern reinforces my institutionalist hesitation: if “the rules of my election are unlawful” suffices without contest-specific facts, federal courts become routine overseers of state vote-counting mechanics pre-election. The narrow, legitimacy-protecting course remains to affirm for lack of standing and leave the Election Day statutes’ merits for a case with district-tethered allegations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not require certainty of defeat and that a candidate’s stake is more particularized than the statewide grievance in Gill v. Whitford. But his reframing of the injury as “forced participation in an unlawful counting regime” still depends, on these pleadings, on a contingent chain—how many ballots arrive late, where they are cast, and whether they matter in these candidates’ races—and Clapper and TransUnion require more than an abstract possibility to establish a “substantial risk” of concrete harm. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, this is not a pre-enforcement posture where the State is regulating petitioners’ conduct or credibly threatening enforcement; the alleged harm comes only through third-party voting behavior and margin sensitivity, yet the complaint lacks district-tethered facts (historical volumes, plausible closeness) to make the risk non-speculative. Accepting standing on this record would, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, supply no limiting principle and effectively invite federal courts into generalized supervision of state election mechanics.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not require candidates to prove a razor-thin margin or probable defeat, and that election rules can impose an imminent, contest-specific burden. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, this is not a pre-enforcement setting where petitioners face a direct legal constraint or enforcement threat; the asserted competitive injury still turns on contingencies about how many late ballots arrive, where they are, and whether they matter in the petitioners’ own races, which Clapper and TransUnion require us to treat as too speculative on this record. Gill v. Whitford’s particularization requirement reinforces that we cannot convert a generalized objection to statewide election administration into standing for specific candidates absent plausibly pleaded, race-tethered facts. Pragmatically, accepting standing here without that limiting principle would predictably invite disruptive pre-election federal litigation over routine election mechanics without a concrete, imminent stake.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury that is actual or imminent, not conjectural, and Petitioners’ alleged harms—vote dilution, increased risk of loss, and added campaign expenditures—are too speculative on this record because they depend on whether a small subset of ballots received after Election Day (but cast by Election Day under 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c)) would materially affect the outcome in any particular federal race. Under Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, a plaintiff cannot manufacture standing by incurring costs to avert a feared injury that is not “certainly impending,” and generalized uncertainty about election administration does not suffice. Gill v. Whitford reinforces that federal courts do not entertain abstract election-law grievances without a plaintiff-specific, particularized injury, and recognizing standing here risks broadening federal judicial supervision of state election administration in a way that threatens institutional legitimacy and federalism. Accordingly, I would affirm dismissal for lack of standing without reaching the merits of the federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, and a candidate subject to an election’s vote-counting rules plausibly alleges an imminent, personal competitive injury when the State plans to count ballots received after the congressionally fixed Election Day. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), and Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, 573 U.S. 149 (2014), forward-looking relief is available where there is a sufficiently imminent and substantial risk of future injury; the federally designated Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)) make the alleged injury to candidates from counting late-received ballots neither abstract nor generalized. Petitioners are not asserting an undifferentiated grievance like the statewide claims rejected in Gill v. Whitford, 585 U.S. 48 (2018), but a candidate-specific harm tied to the rules that determine which votes are counted in their federal races, and the injury is redressable by an injunction requiring compliance with the federal date. Whether a race is “close” goes to degree, not the existence of a cognizable imminent risk, and Article III does not demand proof of certain defeat before suit can be brought.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete and particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not conjectural, and petitioners’ theory largely reduces to an abstract objection to Illinois’s vote-by-mail receipt rule without plausible allegations that the challenged practice creates a non-speculative, outcome-relevant risk to their own races. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, risk-of-harm and procedural-injury theories cannot substitute for a real-world harm unless the risk is sufficiently imminent and concrete; here, the asserted “competitive” injury is too indeterminate absent facts showing that counting ballots received up to 14 days after Election Day (10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c)) is likely to affect petitioners’ electoral prospects in their specific contests. The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)) establish a uniform day for holding elections, but they do not automatically confer standing on any candidate to litigate generalized disputes about ballot administration. Gill v. Whitford reinforces that standing is not satisfied by a generalized grievance about election rules; the plaintiff must show a personal, district-specific injury rather than an institutional objection to how votes are counted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized, and non-speculative injury, and petitioners’ allegations largely reduce to a generalized objection to Illinois’s ballot-receipt rule rather than a showing that these candidates face a substantial, imminent risk of losing or other concrete harm traceable to 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c). Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, probabilistic or risk-based theories cannot rest on conjecture untethered to real-world likelihood, and here the pleadings provide no district-specific facts (margins, volume of affected ballots, historical rates) that would make the asserted “vote dilution/offset” injury plausible rather than abstract. Gill v. Whitford reinforces that courts must not entertain broadly framed election-administration grievances without a plaintiff-specific injury, and the asserted campaign-monitoring or strategy costs are self-inflicted responses to a policy dispute unless tied to a concrete, imminent electoral impact. Denying standing here also avoids pushing election disputes into federal court on thin pleadings in ways that predictably chill access to the ballot for voters who rely on the State’s rules, particularly those facing mail delays or other barriers, while leaving room for properly supported challenges in genuinely close or factually substantiated races.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not conjectural, and these candidates have not plausibly alleged that Illinois’s rule—counting a narrow subset of vote-by-mail ballots received up to 14 days after Election Day under 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c)—poses a sufficiently imminent and substantial risk of changing (or otherwise concretely burdening) their electoral prospects in a way traceable to the challenged practice. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez and Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA, a bare assertion that additional ballots might be counted and might “dilute” timely votes is too abstract without factual allegations tying the late-received tranche to a material, non-speculative competitive harm; Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus allows pre-enforcement standing only where the threatened injury is certainly impending or poses a substantial risk plus concrete compliance burdens, which are not adequately pleaded here. Gill v. Whitford reinforces that federal courts do not entertain generalized grievances about election rules untethered to a plaintiff-specific injury, and accepting standing on this record would risk turning any disagreement with election administration into a justiciable controversy. Given the standing deficiency, I would not reach the merits of whether 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1) preclude receipt deadlines extending beyond the federally designated Election Day.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III demands a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not conjectural, and a plaintiff cannot rest on a generalized interest in correct application of election law. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez and Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA, a probabilistic “risk” becomes cognizable only when it is sufficiently imminent and non-speculative; here, absent plausible allegations that the challenged Illinois receipt rule (10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c)) is likely to affect the outcome (or otherwise impose a concrete, candidate-specific burden beyond ordinary campaign strategy), the asserted harms sound in abstract vote-counting grievances and third-party voter treatment. The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. § 1; 2 U.S.C. § 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1; 3 U.S.C. § 21(1)) may supply a legal rule, but they do not relax the Constitution’s case-or-controversy requirement, and standing cannot be manufactured by converting a disagreement over “time, place, and manner” into a judicially enforceable advisory opinion. Gill v. Whitford reinforces that federal courts require plaintiff-specific injury rather than an undifferentiated claim that an election system is unlawful.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)) establish a single federal Election Day, and Illinois’s rule (10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c)) determines which ballots are counted in those federal contests—making candidates at least among the predictable objects of the ballot-counting regime in a way analogous to regulated-party standing recognized in cases like CBS, Inc. v. FCC. Under ordinary Article III principles, candidates plausibly allege concrete, particularized competitive and resource-allocation harms from a counting regime that can change the electorate after the federal deadline; that kind of imminent, election-cycle harm is more than a generalized grievance and is practically suited for pre-election resolution to avoid post-election remedial chaos. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez cautions against abstract risk-based standing, but where the plaintiff is directly affected by the operative rules governing his election, the asserted injury is not merely speculative and does not require proving a razor-thin margin ex ante. Gill v. Whitford’s particularization requirement is satisfied because the injury alleged is candidate-specific—alteration of the rules for counting votes in their own races—rather than a statewide policy objection in the abstract.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not conjectural, and petitioners’ theory—that counting a limited set of ballots received after Election Day creates a generalized “competitive harm” without plausible allegations that such ballots create a substantial risk of affecting any petitioner’s election—falls short under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), and related imminence principles. Unlike pre-enforcement cases where threatened enforcement against the plaintiff is concrete and targeted, here the asserted injury depends on multiple contingencies (volume of late-arriving ballots, their legality, and their distribution among candidates), and Gill v. Whitford, 585 U.S. 48 (2018), cautions against standing based on undifferentiated harms not shown to affect the plaintiff in a personal and individual way. The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)) may supply a rule of decision on the merits, but they do not themselves establish standing absent a concrete stake in the outcome, and petitioners have not plausibly alleged the “substantial risk” of election-altering harm required for forward-looking relief. Allowing standing on these pleadings would risk converting federal courts into forums for generalized oversight of election administration, contrary to our careful limits on risk-of-harm and procedural-injury standing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not a generalized objection to how an election is administered, and these pleadings do not plausibly allege that Illinois’s 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c) creates a “substantial risk” of electoral harm to these candidates rather than a speculative possibility. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, a probabilistic or forward-looking injury can support injunctive relief only when the risk is sufficiently imminent and substantial, and the candidates’ asserted vote-dilution/competitive-harm theories are untethered to district-specific facts suggesting late-arriving ballots could meaningfully affect their races. Gill v. Whitford reinforces that standing must be plaintiff-specific and not an abstract claim about the legality of election rules, and accepting standing here would invite broad pre-election challenges without a limiting principle. Whatever the merits of the federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)), this record does not show the concrete, non-speculative injury needed to hale state election administration into federal court.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal candidates have Article III standing to challenge Illinois’s policy of counting mail ballots received after the federally prescribed Election Day when those ballots are postmarked (or certified as) on or before Election Day.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Day statutes: 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 (setting a single day for congressional elections) and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1) (presidential election timing), as applied against Illinois’s late-received mail-ballot counting rule, 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c) (2025), and the Article III standing requirement (U.S. Const. art. III).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (federal candidates) argue they are proper parties to sue because Illinois’s post–Election Day receipt deadline alters the legally required rules of the electoral contest in a way that concretely injures candidates: it forces them to compete under an allegedly unlawful ballot-counting regime that can dilute timely votes and increase the risk of an adverse electoral outcome, and it also imposes predictable campaign and resource burdens (monitoring, curing, recount posture, litigation readiness). They contend this is not a request for an election-specific standing doctrine, but an application of ordinary standing principles recognizing injury when a plaintiff is an object of the challenged regulatory scheme (here, the election administration rules governing how votes are counted for the candidate’s contest). They further emphasize that if candidates lack standing, challenges will be pushed into post-election emergencies with severe remedial complications and reliance concerns.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Illinois election officials) argue candidates generally lack Article III standing because the asserted harms are too speculative and generalized: the possibility that late-arriving ballots might change a result is uncertain and depends on multiple contingencies (margin, distribution of votes, number of late ballots, etc.). They characterize the relevant ‘object’ of the late-receipt rule as voters (who are given additional time for ballot receipt), not candidates, and contend candidates cannot manufacture standing from abstract disagreement with election procedures or from non-particularized ‘electoral-system’ grievances. They also argue that without specific factual allegations showing a substantial likelihood of outcome-determinative harm in a particular race, the case fails the concrete-injury and imminence requirements under modern standing doctrine (including limits on ‘procedural’ injuries).
key_precedents: Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510 (1925)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that Article III does not demand proof that the challenged rule will be outcome-determinative, and his point that candidates are more particularized plaintiffs than the voters in Gill has force. But the strongest pro-standing theory—Justice Kavanaugh’s competitive-injury framing—still depends on a speculative chain (late-ballot volume, partisan skew, race margin) that Clapper and TransUnion require us to treat as insufficient on this record, and the “monitoring/litigation readiness” expenditures look like the sort of anticipatory, plaintiff-incurred costs Clapper warns cannot bootstrap standing when the underlying harm is conjectural. Accepting Thomas’s broader “object of the regime” theory here would lack a limiting principle and risk converting generalized “rules of the game” disputes into justiciable controversies, in tension with Gill’s institutional warning. A narrow affirmance on standing best preserves judicial minimalism and avoids deciding the fraught Election Day preemption question without a plaintiff who can plead a substantial, contest-specific risk of concrete harm.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Clapper/TransUnion objection is the strongest point, but it assumes Article III requires a race-specific showing that late ballots will likely alter the outcome; that is not the original public meaning of “case” or “controversy,” and it improperly collapses injury into merits-level proof of vote-total effects. Unlike Gill’s generalized voter grievance, these candidates are directly subjected to an allegedly unlawful counting period that predictably and presently extends the election contest itself, imposing concrete competitive and administrative burdens traceable to the State’s rule rather than to plaintiffs’ “self-inflicted” choices. Justice Alito and Justice Barrett are right to worry about manufactured standing, but Clapper’s mitigation-cost principle fits poorly where the government has itself created the extended post–Election Day window and thereby forces campaigns to respond in real time to protect their legally cognizable interest in a timely, lawfully conducted election. I therefore would reach the merits rather than allow standing doctrine to insulate alleged violations of federal Election Day statutes from pre-election review.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not demand outcome-determinative proof and that candidates are more particularized plaintiffs than the voters in Gill, but his “object of the regime” theory lacks a limiting principle here because the receipt rule regulates election officials and voter eligibility rather than candidates’ conduct or exposure to enforcement. Under Clapper, campaigns cannot create standing by spending money to mitigate a feared harm when that harm still depends on multiple contingencies, and Justice Roberts is right that the record offers no race-specific allegations about late-ballot volume, partisan distribution, or expected margins to satisfy TransUnion’s substantial-risk requirement for forward-looking relief. Justice Kavanaugh’s competitive-injury framing usefully highlights practical burdens, but as he now acknowledges, treating ordinary monitoring and litigation-readiness costs as concrete injury would effectively let any candidate challenge any statewide election-administration rule, collapsing Gill’s bar on generalized “rules of the game” grievances. I therefore would affirm on standing and avoid reaching the preemption merits in the absence of a plaintiff with a concrete, non-speculative, contest-specific stake.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that candidates need not prove outcome-determinative harm and that the State’s counting regime predictably imposes campaign burdens, but that reframing still runs into Clapper’s and TransUnion’s requirement that forward-looking relief rest on a non-speculative, contest-specific substantial risk of concrete injury. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the alleged harm here depends on contingencies—volume of late ballots, partisan skew, and margin—yet the pleadings offer no race-by-race facts to make that risk imminent rather than conjectural. The “monitoring/litigation readiness” costs Thomas treats as compelled by the rule look, under Clapper, like anticipatory expenditures that cannot bootstrap standing when the underlying electoral harm remains uncertain. Given Gill’s warning against generalized “rules of the game” disputes, Article III restraint counsels affirmance on standing without reaching the preemption merits on this record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that candidates are not asserting a Gill-style voter generalized grievance and need not prove outcome-determinative harm. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the asserted “competitive injury” still depends on a speculative chain—unknown late-ballot volume, partisan skew, and margin—and TransUnion/Clapper require more than campaign precautions taken in response to that uncertainty. Treating monitoring, recount posture, and litigation readiness as present injury would effectively let any candidate challenge any statewide election-administration rule, which is exactly the limiting-principle problem Justice Gorsuch identifies and would collapse Gill’s restraint on “rules of the game” disputes. Because this record lacks contest-specific allegations showing a substantial risk of concrete harm traceable to the receipt rule, I would affirm on standing and not reach the Election Day preemption merits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not demand proof that the challenged rule will be outcome-determinative in a particular race, and that candidates are more particularized plaintiffs than the voters in Gill. But even accepting that premise, Clapper and TransUnion still require a non-speculative, substantial risk of concrete harm, and on this record the asserted competitive injury depends on contingencies (late-ballot volume, partisan skew, and margin) not alleged in any contest-specific way, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize. The monitoring/litigation-readiness costs Thomas would treat as compelled burdens look, under Clapper, like anticipatory expenditures that cannot supply standing when the underlying harm remains conjectural; otherwise any candidate could manufacture standing to challenge virtually any statewide “rule of the game,” collapsing Gill’s generalized-grievance limit. Given separation-of-powers constraints, I would not reach the Election Day preemption merits without a plaintiff who plausibly alleges a concrete and imminent risk tied to their race rather than an abstract objection to Illinois’s counting rules.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that candidates need not plead outcome-determinative harm and that the State’s counting regime predictably forces campaigns to incur monitoring and recount-response burdens. But as the Chief Justice explains, Clapper and TransUnion still require a substantial, non-speculative risk of concrete harm for forward-looking relief, and this record is missing race-specific allegations about likely late-ballot volume, partisan skew, or margins, making the claimed competitive injury too contingent and abstract. I agree with Justice Barrett that this is unlike SBA List because the receipt rule does not regulate or threaten enforcement against candidates, so the pre-enforcement analogy does not supply a limiting principle. Under Gill’s generalized-grievance constraint and an institutionalist preference for narrow rulings, I would affirm on standing and avoid reaching the contentious preemption merits without a plaintiff alleging a contest-specific, imminent risk.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not require petitioners to show the challenged rule will be outcome-determinative, and that candidates are more particularized plaintiffs than the voters in Gill. But even accepting that premise, Clapper and TransUnion still require a non-speculative, substantial risk of concrete harm for forward-looking relief, and here the asserted “competitive” injury depends on contingencies (late-ballot volume, partisan skew, margin) not pleaded in a race-specific way; as Chief Justice Roberts notes, the monitoring and litigation-readiness costs look like anticipatory expenditures that cannot bootstrap standing when the underlying risk remains conjectural. Thomas’s “object of the regime” framing also stretches our regulated-party/pre-enforcement cases (e.g., Susan B. Anthony List), because this receipt rule primarily directs election officials and expands what ballots are counted rather than constraining candidates’ conduct or threatening them with enforcement. A narrow affirmance on standing preserves Article III limits and avoids reaching the preemption merits without a plaintiff showing a concrete, imminent, contest-specific injury.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Article III does not require a plaintiff to prove ex ante that an election rule will be outcome-determinative, and that candidates are more particularized plaintiffs than the voters in Gill. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito correctly respond that TransUnion still demands a substantial, non-speculative risk of concrete harm for forward-looking relief, and on this record the asserted downstream injury depends on multiple contingencies (late-ballot volume, partisan split, and margin) without race-specific allegations. Nor do Justice Thomas’s “object of the regime” and Justice Kavanaugh’s earlier competitive-injury framing overcome Clapper’s constraint that self-incurred monitoring/litigation-readiness costs cannot bootstrap standing when the underlying risk remains conjectural, especially where the receipt rule regulates election officials rather than candidates in the SBA List sense. Prudentially and procedurally, I remain persuaded that reaching preemption here would invite federal courts to adjudicate generalized “rules of the game” disputes in tension with Gill’s limiting principle.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete and imminent injury, and petitioners’ theory—that counting a universe of late-arriving ballots might dilute timely votes or change an outcome—rests on a chain of contingencies about how many such ballots will be received, how they will be cast, and whether they will be outcome-determinative, making the alleged harm too speculative under Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez. Unlike pre-enforcement cases involving a credible threat of prosecution, see Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, petitioners are not facing enforcement or a compelled choice backed by sanction; they object to how the State counts ballots cast by third parties. Gill v. Whitford underscores that generalized grievances about the “rules of the game” do not suffice absent district- or candidate-specific facts showing particularized harm, and on this record petitioners have not plausibly alleged a “substantial risk” of electoral injury tied to their races. A narrow disposition dismissing for lack of standing avoids reaching the federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)) and preserves institutional legitimacy by not deciding a nationally consequential election-administration question in the absence of a proper plaintiff.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury, but it does not demand certainty of ultimate electoral defeat; a substantial risk of competitive harm can suffice where the plaintiff is an object of the challenged governmental regime. Here, Illinois’ rule governs how votes are counted in the very contest in which petitioners are candidates, and the predictable need to monitor and respond to a post–Election Day counting period constitutes a concrete burden traceable to the rule and redressable by enjoining enforcement. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez confirms that standing cannot rest on abstraction alone, yet this is not a generalized grievance like Gill v. Whitford; it is a candidate-specific competitive injury stemming from the administration of his election under an allegedly unlawful timing rule that conflicts with the federal “single day” command in 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1. Because the alleged injury arises from being subjected to an election regime that changes the competitive conditions of the contest, petitioners have standing to sue.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not one resting on a speculative chain of contingencies. Here the candidates’ asserted harms—vote dilution and increased risk of an adverse outcome from ballots received after Election Day—depend on uncertain future events (number of late ballots, partisan distribution, margin of victory), which is precisely the kind of probabilistic theory Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA rejects, and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez underscores that forward-looking relief demands a sufficiently imminent and substantial risk of harm. The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)) regulate the timing of elections, but they do not themselves confer standing absent a plaintiff-specific injury; treating any candidate as an “object” of all election-administration rules would invite generalized grievances akin to those disallowed in Gill v. Whitford. Because petitioners have not pleaded race-specific facts showing a substantial likelihood of concrete harm traceable to Illinois’s receipt rule and redressable by an injunction, I would affirm dismissal for lack of standing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete and particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not a speculative chain of contingencies about how many late-arriving ballots might be received and how they might affect any given race. Under Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA, petitioners’ asserted future harm—an increased risk of electoral defeat and attendant campaign expenditures to monitor or litigate—does not meet the “certainly impending” standard and cannot be manufactured through self-inflicted costs taken to avert hypothetical harm. Their claim also resembles the kind of generalized, undifferentiated grievance Gill v. Whitford rejected where plaintiffs fail to tie the challenged rule to a personal, outcome-linked injury in a particular contest. Because standing fails, we do not reach whether 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1) preempt Illinois’s receipt-deadline rule, 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is certainly impending or poses a substantial risk, and the candidates’ asserted harm here depends on multiple contingencies—how many late-arriving ballots there will be, how they break, and whether they affect any race outcome—making it too speculative under Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez. Unlike the pre-enforcement “credible threat” cases such as Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, Illinois’s late-receipt rule does not regulate candidates’ conduct or threaten them with enforcement; it primarily confers a benefit on voters and any alleged “vote dilution” is not tied to a personal, outcome-likely injury rather than a generalized objection to election administration (cf. Gill v. Whitford). Without district- or race-specific allegations showing a substantial risk of concrete harm traceable to counting these ballots and redressable by an injunction, the federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1)) cannot be reached because standing is absent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized, and non-speculative injury, and petitioners’ theory rests on a chain of contingencies—how many ballots arrive after Election Day, how they break, and whether they matter in the result—making the alleged harm too conjectural under Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez. Unlike the pre-enforcement setting in Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, there is no credible threat of enforcement action directed at candidates, and candidates are not the primary objects of Illinois’s receipt rule (10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c)); the asserted “vote dilution” is a generalized grievance about election administration akin to the districtwide, non-individualized harm rejected in Gill v. Whitford. Petitioners also have not pleaded facts showing a substantial risk of outcome-determinative injury in their particular races, and Article III does not permit courts to adjudicate abstract disputes about whether 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1) preempt a state’s ballot-receipt deadline absent a plaintiff with a concrete stake. Whatever the merits of the federal Election Day statutes’ meaning, separation of powers demands we respect the standing limits that keep federal courts from resolving such policy disagreements in the abstract.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I would hold the candidates have Article III standing because Illinois’s vote-counting rule governs the rules of the electoral contest in which they are competing and predictably forces them to incur concrete, particularized burdens (monitoring, litigation readiness, recount posture) and to face a nontrivial risk of competitive harm from ballots counted after the federal Election Day set by 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1). Our standing cases do not require a plaintiff to plead that the challenged practice will be outcome-determinative; rather, the inquiry is whether the plaintiff faces a real, concrete injury, consistent with TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez’s concreteness requirement. This fits comfortably with the Court’s long-recognized “competitive injury/object of the regulatory regime” principle (as in cases like Pierce v. Society of Sisters) and avoids pushing challenges into post-election thickets with serious remedial and reliance problems—an important practical consideration for institutional legitimacy. Gill v. Whitford’s bar on generalized grievances is not violated because the injury alleged is tied to these plaintiffs’ own candidacies and the vote-counting rules that determine their elections.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury that is actual or imminent, not one that depends on a speculative chain of contingencies; here, the candidates’ asserted harm from Illinois’ post–Election Day receipt rule turns on uncertain facts about how many late ballots will arrive, how they will break, and whether they will affect any petitioner’s race, falling short under Clapper’s “certainly impending”/“substantial risk” standard as applied in TransUnion’s insistence on concrete injury. The generalized claim that allegedly unlawful counting “dilutes” lawful votes resembles the kind of undifferentiated, systemwide grievance this Court rejected as insufficiently particularized in Gill v. Whitford. To the extent petitioners rely on campaign expenditures and monitoring costs, those look self-inflicted responses to a feared future loss rather than injuries caused by the challenged statute itself, again tracking Clapper. Because standing fails, we need not reach whether 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1) preempt Illinois’ 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c) (2025).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete and particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not an abstract disagreement with how Illinois runs elections, and the candidates’ asserted harms here hinge on contingencies about how many late-arriving ballots will be received and how they will break. Under Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA and Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, forward-looking standing can rest on a “certainly impending” injury or a “substantial risk” of harm, but the pleadings described in the record reflect an insufficiently grounded showing of substantial, race-specific risk (as Justice Sotomayor’s questioning highlighted), making the claimed “vote dilution/outcome risk” too speculative. Nor do the asserted monitoring and litigation-readiness costs convert an undifferentiated electoral-system grievance into a concrete injury under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, which cautions against treating generalized or procedural complaints as Article III injuries absent a real-world harm closely tied to the plaintiff. Because standing is lacking, the Court should not reach whether 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1) preempt Illinois’s receipt-deadline rule, 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c).
